passage:
Monday. Kalyani watched Ritu explain the lab results so clearly that even the teacher wrote it down. Kalyani kept her own half-finished graphs closed under her notebook. "Mine aren't ready," she said.

Thursday. She stayed back after class. "How did you make your graphs so easy to read?" Ritu showed her two tricks. Kalyani felt a small sting of envy, but she wrote both down.

Next Tuesday. Kalyani shared her graphs with the group. They were not as sharp as Ritu's, but the axis labels were clear. Ritu smiled. "Yours make my section easier to follow."

qa.q: What did Kalyani say when she hid her graphs on Monday?
What was Kalyani feeling on Thursday when she asked Ritu for help?
qa.a: She felt a small sting of envy but still wanted to learn, so she wrote both tricks down.

qa.q: What changed in how Kalyani handled her work between Monday and Tuesday?
qa.a: She stopped hiding it, learned from Ritu and shared her own graphs with clear labels.

qa.q: How might Ritu see being asked for tricks?
qa.a: Ritu probably feels respected, and her comment that Kalyani's graphs help her section shows the group benefits.

grounding: A groupmate who is better than the protagonist prompts envy, but she learns from them and does her own part.

passage:
"Salma, can I see your part of the report?" Ritu asked, pulling up a chair in the reading room.
Salma closed her laptop halfway. "It's not ready."
It was ready. It just looked thin next to Ritu's section, which had diagrams, three case studies and a professor's comment saying "excellent".
Ritu raised an eyebrow. "We submit in two days."
Salma sighed and opened the laptop. "Okay. Honestly? I didn't want you to see it because yours is so good. I felt stupid."
"Mine took four drafts," Ritu said. "You didn't see those."
"Four?"
"Four. Want me to show you how I found the case studies? It's one database."
"Yes. Please."
They sat for an hour. Salma found two case studies of her own and rewrote her opening.
"Better?" she asked.
"Better. And now it sounds like you, not me."

qa.q: How many drafts did Ritu's section take?
Why did Salma close her laptop halfway?
qa.a: She felt envious and stupid next to Ritu's excellent section and didn't want her work seen.

qa.q: How did Salma turn the envy into learning?
qa.a: She admitted it, asked Ritu to show her the database, found her own case studies and rewrote her opening.

qa.q: How does Ritu see Salma's work?
qa.a: As worth improving and truly Salma's own; Ritu shares the method and says it now sounds like Salma.

grounding: Shows envy of a stronger groupmate and choosing to learn from her and do one's own part well instead of hiding the work.

passage:
In our architecture studio, Kiran was the star. Kiran's models got pinned on the wall; mine got polite nods. In our group project on a bus shelter, I started doing a strange thing: I worked on my sketches at night and didn't upload them to the shared folder until the last minute, so nobody could compare.
Two days before the review, Kiran messaged me: "Your roof idea from the first meeting was great. Why haven't you put it in?"
I stared at that message for a long time. Kiran had remembered my idea. I'd been hiding it out of envy.
I uploaded everything that night. Kiran built the roof into the model and asked me how I'd thought of the rain channel. I asked Kiran how to make cleaner joints. We swapped for an hour.
At the review, the jury said the roof was the best part. I'd nearly kept it in a drawer.
— Aparna

qa.q: What was the group project about?
Why did Aparna keep the sketches out of the shared folder?
qa.a: Aparna felt envious of Kiran and afraid of being compared.
Aparna uploaded everything, and the two swapped skills: the roof and rain channel idea for Kiran's cleaner joints.

qa.q: How did Kiran see Aparna's work?
qa.a: As valuable; Kiran remembered the roof idea and wanted it in the model.

grounding: Illustrates envy of a star groupmate leading to hiding one's work, and learning from them and contributing fully instead.
